Lecture 32

Separation of variables and a finite string

Lecture objectives

We find the modes of the string with fixed ends and prove a theorem on sine series: mean-square convergence for piecewise continuous functions, pointwise convergence for piecewise C1C^1C1 functions and uniform convergence for continuous piecewise C1C^1C1 functions that vanish at the ends. We then solve the string, share its energy among the modes and interpret a plucked string.

Lecture 31 solved the string on the whole line and on a half-line. A guitar string has two fixed ends. In this lecture we describe its motion as a sum of standing waves, the normal modes of the string. The lecture reads in four stages: the modes and the coefficients (Sections 32.1–32.2), the theorem on sine series (Section 32.3), the string solved, with its energy (Sections 32.4–32.6), and a plucked string (Section 32.7).

32.1 Separated solutions and the modes

Throughout the lecture L>0L>0L>0 and c>0,c>0c>0, and the string with fixed ends is the problem utt=c2uxx(0<x<L, t>0),u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0(t≥0),u(x,0)=u0(x),ut(x,0)=v0(x)(0≤x≤L).\begin{gathered} u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}\quad(0<x<L,\ t>0),\qquad u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0\quad(t\ge0),\\ u(x,0)=u_0(x),\quad u_t(x,0)=v_0(x)\quad(0\le x\le L). \end{gathered}utt​=c2uxx​(0<x<L, t>0),u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0(t≥0),u(x,0)=u0​(x),ut​(x,0)=v0​(x)(0≤x≤L).​(32.1) It is Lecture 29’s string with f=0f=0f=0 and fixed ends. Separation of variables first seeks solutions of the equation and the boundary conditions, without the data, that are products u(x,t)=y(x) q(t),u(x,t)=y(x)\,q(t),u(x,t)=y(x)q(t),(32.2) with yyy twice continuously differentiable on [0,L][0,L][0,L] and not identically zero, and qqq twice continuously differentiable on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) and not identically zero on (0,∞).(0,\infty)(0,∞). Separation leads to the following eigenvalue problem.

Definition 32.1 (Eigenvalue and eigenfunction). A number λ∈C\lambda\in\Cλ∈C is an eigenvalue of the fixed-end problem if −y′′=λyon (0,L),y(0)=y(L)=0,-y''=\lambda y\quad\text{on }(0,L),\qquad y(0)=y(L)=0,−y′′=λyon (0,L),y(0)=y(L)=0, has a solution y,yy, twice continuously differentiable on [0,L][0,L][0,L] and not identically zero. For λ=λn\lambda=\lambda_nλ=λn​ the time factor solves q¨=−ωn2q\ddot q=-\omega_n^2qq¨​=−ωn2​q with ωn=ckn=nπcL.\omega_n=ck_n=\frac{n\pi c}L .ωn​=ckn​=Lnπc​.(32.6) So the separated solutions are the normal modes un(x,t)=sin⁡(knx)(αncos⁡(ωnt)+βnsin⁡(ωnt)),u_n(x,t)=\sin(k_nx)\bigl(\alpha_n\cos(\omega_nt)+\beta_n\sin(\omega_nt)\bigr),un​(x,t)=sin(kn​x)(αn​cos(ωn​t)+βn​sin(ωn​t)),(32.7) with real constants αn\alpha_nαn​ and βn,\beta_nβn​, defined for every real t.tt. A mode is a standing wave. Its shape sin⁡(knx)\sin(k_nx)sin(kn​x) does not move, and only its amplitude oscillates with the angular frequency ωn.\omega_nωn​. The mode nnn has n−1n-1n−1 interior nodes, the points x=jL/nx=jL/nx=jL/n with 0<j<n,0<j<n0<j<n, where it is always at rest (Figure 32.1). Its frequency νn=ωn/(2π)=nc/(2L)\nu_n=\omega_n/(2\pi)=nc/(2L)νn​=ωn​/(2π)=nc/(2L) is an integer multiple of the lowest frequency ν1=c/(2L),\nu_1=c/(2L)ν1​=c/(2L), and these multiples are the harmonics. The lowest mode has the period 2L/c,2L/c2L/c, the time for a signal to run to the far end and back, as Lecture 29 stated.

Finitely many masses in Lecture 14 had finitely many modes. A string has infinitely many, so we try the series u(x,t)=∑n=1∞sin⁡(knx)(αncos⁡(ωnt)+βnsin⁡(ωnt)).u(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(k_nx)\bigl(\alpha_n\cos(\omega_nt)+\beta_n\sin(\omega_nt)\bigr).u(x,t)=n=1∑∞​sin(kn​x)(αn​cos(ωn​t)+βn​sin(ωn​t)).(32.8) At t=0,t=0t=0, formally, u0(x)=∑nαnsin⁡(knx)u_0(x)=\sum_n\alpha_n\sin(k_nx)u0​(x)=∑n​αn​sin(kn​x) and v0(x)=∑nωnβnsin⁡(knx).v_0(x)=\sum_n\omega_n\beta_n\sin(k_nx)v0​(x)=∑n​ωn​βn​sin(kn​x). This raises two questions: which functions are sums of sine series, with which coefficients, and when the series may be differentiated term by term so that its sum solves the equation. Sections 32.2–32.3 answer the first and Sections 32.4–32.5 the second.

32.2 Orthogonality and sine coefficients

We use Lecture 23’s piecewise continuous and piecewise C1C^1C1 functions on [0,L],[0,L][0,L], where the partition into pieces is finite. A piecewise continuous function on [0,L][0,L][0,L] is bounded. As in Lecture 25, the inner product and the norm on (0,L)(0,L)(0,L) are ⟨f,g⟩=∫0Lf(x)‾ g(x) ⁣dx,∥f∥=(∫0L∣f(x)∣2 ⁣dx)1/2,\inner fg=\int_0^L\conj{f(x)}\,g(x)\dd x,\qquad \norm f=\Bigl(\int_0^L\abs{f(x)}^2\dd x\Bigr)^{1/2},⟨f,g⟩=∫0L​f(x)​g(x)dx,∥f∥=(∫0L​∣f(x)∣2dx)1/2,(32.9) and two functions that differ only at finitely many points have the same inner products and the same norm. As in Lecture 25, we identify such functions when we use this inner product and norm. Lecture 25’s Cauchy–Schwarz lemma, applied to fff and ggg extended by zero outside [0,L],[0,L][0,L], gives ∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤∥f∥∥g∥.\abs{\inner fg}\le\norm f\norm g∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤∥f∥∥g∥. Expanding ∥f+g∥2=∥f∥2+2Re⁡⟨f,g⟩+∥g∥2≤(∥f∥+∥g∥)2\norm{f+g}^2=\norm f^2+2\Re\inner fg+\norm g^2\le(\norm f+\norm g)^2∥f+g∥2=∥f∥2+2Re⟨f,g⟩+∥g∥2≤(∥f∥+∥g∥)2 gives the triangle inequality ∥f+g∥≤∥f∥+∥g∥.\norm{f+g}\le\norm f+\norm g∥f+g∥≤∥f∥+∥g∥. The sines are orthogonal. For integers m,n≥1,m,n\ge1m,n≥1, the identity 2sin⁡(kmx)sin⁡(knx)=cos⁡((km−kn)x)−cos⁡((km+kn)x)2\sin(k_mx)\sin(k_nx)=\cos((k_m-k_n)x)-\cos((k_m+k_n)x)2sin(km​x)sin(kn​x)=cos((km​−kn​)x)−cos((km​+kn​)x) gives ∫0Lsin⁡(kmx)sin⁡(knx) ⁣dx=L2 δmn,∫0Lcos⁡(kmx)cos⁡(knx) ⁣dx=L2 δmn,\int_0^L\sin(k_mx)\sin(k_nx)\dd x=\frac L2\,\delta_{mn},\qquad \int_0^L\cos(k_mx)\cos(k_nx)\dd x=\frac L2\,\delta_{mn},∫0L​sin(km​x)sin(kn​x)dx=2L​δmn​,∫0L​cos(km​x)cos(kn​x)dx=2L​δmn​,(32.10) because ∫0Lcos⁡(kjx) ⁣dx=0\int_0^L\cos(k_jx)\dd x=0∫0L​cos(kj​x)dx=0 for every integer j≠0.j\ne0j=0. The second identity follows in the same way from 2cos⁡(kmx)cos⁡(knx)=cos⁡((km−kn)x)+cos⁡((km+kn)x).2\cos(k_mx)\cos(k_nx)=\cos((k_m-k_n)x)+\cos((k_m+k_n)x)2cos(km​x)cos(kn​x)=cos((km​−kn​)x)+cos((km​+kn​)x). So the functions en(x)=2/L sin⁡(knx),e_n(x)=\sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(k_nx)en​(x)=2/L​sin(kn​x), n≥1,n\ge1n≥1, are orthonormal, ⟨em,en⟩=δmn.\inner{e_m}{e_n}=\delta_{mn}⟨em​,en​⟩=δmn​. As in LA 8, we take the inner product ⟨en,f⟩\inner{e_n}f⟨en​,f⟩ as the coefficient of en.e_nen​.

Definition 32.3 (Sine and cosine coefficients). For fff piecewise continuous on [0,L][0,L][0,L] the sine coefficients and the cosine coefficients are bn(f)=2L∫0Lf(x)sin⁡(knx) ⁣dx(n≥1),an(f)=2L∫0Lf(x)cos⁡(knx) ⁣dx(n≥0).b_n(f)=\frac2L\int_0^Lf(x)\sin(k_nx)\dd x\quad(n\ge1),\qquad a_n(f)=\frac2L\int_0^Lf(x)\cos(k_nx)\dd x\quad(n\ge0).bn​(f)=L2​∫0L​f(x)sin(kn​x)dx(n≥1),an​(f)=L2​∫0L​f(x)cos(kn​x)dx(n≥0).(32.11) The partial sums of the sine series of fff are SNf(x)=∑n=1Nbn(f)sin⁡(knx),S_Nf(x)=\sum_{n=1}^Nb_n(f)\sin(k_nx)SN​f(x)=∑n=1N​bn​(f)sin(kn​x), N=1,2,….N=1,2,\ldotsN=1,2,….

Thus bn(f)sin⁡(knx)=⟨en,f⟩en(x),b_n(f)\sin(k_nx)=\inner{e_n}fe_n(x)bn​(f)sin(kn​x)=⟨en​,f⟩en​(x), and the coefficients are forced if a series converges uniformly.

Proposition 32.4 (Coefficients of a uniformly convergent series). If the series ∑nγnsin⁡(knx)\sum_n\gamma_n\sin(k_nx)∑n​γn​sin(kn​x) converges uniformly on [0,L][0,L][0,L] to a function f,ff, then γn=bn(f)\gamma_n=b_n(f)γn​=bn​(f) for every n≥1.n\ge1n≥1.

Proof. The terms are continuous, so fff is continuous (GM 30). Multiply the series by sin⁡(kmx).\sin(k_mx)sin(km​x). It still converges uniformly, because ∣sin⁡∣≤1.\abs{\sin}\le1∣sin∣≤1. By GM 30’s theorem on the integration of a uniform limit, applied to the real and the imaginary parts, the integral of fsin⁡(kmx)f\sin(k_mx)fsin(km​x) is the sum of the integrals of the terms, and by (32.10) only the term n=mn=mn=m contributes: ∫0Lfsin⁡(kmx) ⁣dx=γmL/2.\int_0^Lf\sin(k_mx)\dd x=\gamma_mL/2∫0L​fsin(km​x)dx=γm​L/2. ■

32.3 The theorem on sine series

GM 35 cited the pointwise result for periodic functions. We prove its sine-series form here, with the other convergence statements that the string needs.

Theorem 32.5 (Sine series on (0,L)).(0,L)(0,L)). Let fff be piecewise continuous on [0,L].[0,L][0,L].

  • Best approximation and Bessel’s inequality. For every NNN and all numbers γ1,…,γN,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_Nγ1​,…,γN​, ∥f−∑n=1Nγnsin⁡(knx)∥2=∥f−SNf∥2+L2∑n=1N∣bn(f)−γn∣2,∥f−SNf∥2=∥f∥2−L2∑n=1N∣bn(f)∣2.\begin{aligned} \norm{f-\sum_{n=1}^N\gamma_n\sin(k_nx)}^2&=\norm{f-S_Nf}^2+\frac L2\sum_{n=1}^N\abs{b_n(f)-\gamma_n}^2,\\ \norm{f-S_Nf}^2&=\norm f^2-\frac L2\sum_{n=1}^N\abs{b_n(f)}^2 . \end{aligned}​f−n=1∑N​γn​sin(kn​x)​2∥f−SN​f∥2​=∥f−SN​f∥2+2L​n=1∑N​∣bn​(f)−γn​∣2,=∥f∥2−2L​n=1∑N​∣bn​(f)∣2.​(32.12) In particular L2∑n=1∞∣bn(f)∣2≤∥f∥2.\frac L2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\abs{b_n(f)}^2\le\norm f^22L​∑n=1∞​∣bn​(f)∣2≤∥f∥2. The same holds for the cosine coefficients: L2∑n=1∞∣an(f)∣2≤∥f∥2.\frac L2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\abs{a_n(f)}^2\le\norm f^22L​∑n=1∞​∣an​(f)∣2≤∥f∥2.

Parseval’s identity, equivalently the mean-square convergence of every sine series of a piecewise continuous f,ff, is the completeness of the sines. In particular such an fff with zero sine coefficients is zero off finitely many points. The extension to all square-integrable functions needs the Lebesgue integral (AN 6, the theorem that the sines form an orthonormal basis of L2(0,L)),L^2(0,L)L2(0,L)), and we do not need it.

A guitar string is plucked by pulling one point aside and releasing it, as in Lecture 31’s triangular pluck. Its initial shape has corners, so Theorem 32.9 does not apply. The series still converges, and it gives Lecture 31’s d’Alembert solution.

So the series of a plucked string is the weaker solution that Lecture 31 defined, not a classical one. Its partial sums are classical solutions with the initial data SNu0S_Nu_0SN​u0​ and SNv0,S_Nv_0SN​v0​, and they converge to it uniformly. The termwise second derivatives do not converge in general. On the whole line of Lecture 31 a localized pulse travels away and never returns.

Summary

Separating the variables of a string with fixed ends gives the modes, standing waves with the harmonic frequencies ωn=nπc/L.\omega_n=n\pi c/Lωn​=nπc/L. Sine series converge in the mean square, pointwise and uniformly under increasing hypotheses.

  • Modes: eigenvalues kn2,k_n^2kn2​, kn=nπ/L,k_n=n\pi/Lkn​=nπ/L, eigenfunctions sin⁡(knx);\sin(k_nx)sin(kn​x); the motion has the period 2L/c.2L/c2L/c.

  • Coefficients: bn(f)=2L∫0Lfsin⁡(knx) ⁣dx,b_n(f)=\frac2L\int_0^Lf\sin(k_nx)\dd xbn​(f)=L2​∫0L​fsin(kn​x)dx, forced for a uniformly convergent sine series.

  • Sine series on (0,L):(0,L)(0,L): ∥f−SNf∥→0\norm{f-S_Nf}\to0∥f−SN​f∥→0 and Parseval for piecewise continuous f;ff; the half-sum on (0,L)(0,L)(0,L) for piecewise C1C^1C1 f;ff; uniform convergence for continuous piecewise C1C^1C1 fff with f(0)=f(L)=0.f(0)=f(L)=0f(0)=f(L)=0.

  • Decay: smoothness and vanishing even derivatives at the ends give ∑nm−1∣bn(f)∣<∞.\sum n^{m-1}\abs{b_n(f)}<\infty∑nm−1∣bn​(f)∣<∞.

  • String: for u0∈C2u_0\in C^2u0​∈C2 with u0′′u_0''u0′′​ piecewise C1C^1C1 and v0∈C1v_0\in C^1v0​∈C1 with v0′v_0'v0′​ piecewise C1,C^1C1, under (32.17) the series (32.16) is the unique classical solution in Lecture 31’s class.

  • Energy: E=∑nρL4(ωn2bn(u0)2+bn(v0)2),E=\sum_n\frac{\rho L}4\bigl(\omega_n^2b_n(u_0)^2+b_n(v_0)^2\bigr)E=∑n​4ρL​(ωn2​bn​(u0​)2+bn​(v0​)2), each term constant.

  • Pluck: the series converges uniformly to the d’Alembert solution of the odd 2L2L2L-periodic extensions; its coefficients decay like n−2.n^{-2}n−2.

Lecture 33 solves Laplace’s equation on a rectangle with the same sine series.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. A string of length LLL with wave speed ccc has two fixed ends. Which pair gives its third spatial mode up to a constant factor and its angular frequency?

Hint. Impose zeros at both ends first. Then use the time equation to convert the allowed wave number to angular frequency.

The left end selects a sine, and the right end requires kL=nπkL=n\pikL=nπ. For n=3n=3n=3, the shape is sin⁡(3πx/L)\sin(3\pi x/L)sin(3πx/L) and the time equation gives ω=ck=3πc/L\omega=ck=3\pi c/Lω=ck=3πc/L. A cosine would violate the left condition. The value 3c/(2L)3c/(2L)3c/(2L) is the ordinary frequency in cycles per unit time. The wave number 3π/(2L)3\pi/(2L)3π/(2L) used in the other sine leaves the right end nonzero.

2. On the dimensionless interval 0<x<20<x<20<x<2, expand f(x)=xf(x)=xf(x)=x in the unnormalized sine functions sin⁡(nπx/2)\sin(n\pi x/2)sin(nπx/2). Find the coefficient of the first sine and round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Project onto the first sine and divide by its squared norm over the interval.

The first sine has squared norm L/2=1L/2=1L/2=1. Integration by parts gives ∫02xsin⁡(πx/2) ⁣dx=4/π\int_0^2 x\sin(\pi x/2)\dd x=4/\pi∫02​xsin(πx/2)dx=4/π, since the sine term from integrating the cosine vanishes at both endpoints. This gives 1.27. The sine series takes the value zero at the right endpoint, where fff has the value 222. The coefficient calculation still applies, and the series converges to fff in mean square.

3. A fixed string has zero initial velocity and a triangular initial displacement that vanishes at both ends. Which statement about the sine-mode solution is valid?

Hint. Distinguish convergence of the displacement series from convergence after two differentiations. What regularity does the corner permit?

The continuous piecewise smooth profile with zero end values has a uniformly convergent sine series. The triangular pluck gives the d’Alembert solution of the odd periodic extension. The moving kink can prevent classical second derivatives. The energy uses first derivatives, which exist away from the kinks. At release, Parseval’s identity for the cosine series of the piecewise continuous derivative u0′u_0'u0′​ gives the energy as the sum of modal energies. The lecture’s midpoint example checks this sum explicitly. Zero end values alone do not give the classical theorem’s smoothness hypotheses, and uniform convergence alone does not justify two termwise differentiations.

4. A plucked string starts from rest. Its displacement coefficients satisfy ∣bn∣≤K/n2\abs{b_n}\le K/n^2∣bn​∣≤K/n2 with K>0K>0K>0. Retain the first NNN modes. Starting the comparison integral at NNN, what bound for the absolute displacement error holds uniformly in space and time for every positive mode count?

Hint. Bound each sine and cosine factor in absolute value, then compare the remaining sum with an integral.

Each sine and time cosine has absolute value at most one. The tail is therefore bounded by K∑n>Nn−2≤K∫N∞s−2 ⁣ds=K/NK\sum_{n>N}n^{-2}\le K\int_N^\infty s^{-2}\dd s=K/NK∑n>N​n−2≤K∫N∞​s−2ds=K/N. The bound K/N2K/N^2K/N2 has the size of one term and omits the accumulated tail. Integrating from N+1N+1N+1 gives K/(N+1)K/(N+1)K/(N+1), a lower comparison for the majorant sum. The bound K/(2N)K/(2N)K/(2N) adds an unsupported factor of one half.
